params.text:
What to do if someone falls

Seeing someone fall is alarming, but the safest response is a calm and careful one. Do not rush to lift the person up. Moving someone who has an injury – particularly a possible fracture or spinal injury – can cause serious further harm. Never assume a fall is minor just because the person says they are fine.

Check the situation first

  • Response and breathing: are they conscious and breathing normally? If they are unresponsive or not breathing normally, call 999 and start your emergency procedure.
  • Injury and pain: ask where it hurts and look for bleeding and for signs of a fracture, such as a shortened or turned-out leg, or an obvious deformity.
  • What happened: if they can tell you, find out whether they felt dizzy, blacked out or hit their head.
  • Comfort: reassure them and keep them warm, still and comfortable where they are.

When to call 999

Call 999 for an ambulance if any of these apply, even if the person plays it down:

  • Head injury: they hit their head, or seem drowsy, confused or unwell afterwards.
  • Anticoagulants: they take blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin, apixaban or rivaroxaban, as these can cause dangerous bleeding, including inside the head, after a knock.
  • Suspected fracture: severe pain, an inability to move or bear weight, or a limb that looks wrong.
  • Unresponsive, unwell, or you are simply unsure.

Helping up, and never lifting by hand

If someone may be injured, do not move them, and never lift them from the floor by hand — manual lifting risks worsening a fracture or head injury and can injure you too. Summon a colleague to help, and seek medical help or an ambulance if there is any injury or you are unsure. Only help a person up when you are confident it is safe: if it is safe to raise an uninjured person, use the correct moving-and-handling technique or suitable equipment, such as a raising cushion or hoist, as you have been trained. Keep observing them afterwards, as some effects of a fall appear hours later. Then record and report the fall so its cause can be reviewed.

params.alt: A care worker sitting with an older person they support, who looks worried, beside the heading “What to do if someone falls”. Key points: Response and breathing; Injury and pain; What happened.

params.question: If a person falls, the first thing you should do is quickly lift them back onto their feet.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. You should never rush to lift someone up. Check for injury and get help first, because moving an injured person can make things much worse.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. You should not rush to move them. Check for injury and summon help first, as lifting someone with a fracture or spinal injury can cause serious harm.

params.question: You find a person you support on the floor. They say their hip hurts and cannot move it. What should you do?

answers.text: Keep them still and comfortable, check for injury, and summon medical help without moving them

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pain and inability to move the hip suggest a possible fracture, so keep them still and get medical help before any movement.

answers.text: Help them straight up so they are more comfortable on a chair

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Moving someone with a suspected fracture can cause serious further harm. Keep them still and summon help first.

answers.text: Give them painkillers and carry on with the visit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This ignores a possible serious injury. They need to be kept still and assessed by medical help.

answers.text: Leave them alone while you finish other tasks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The person must not be left. Stay with them, reassure them, keep them still and summon help.

params.question: You find Mr Adeyemi on his bedroom floor. He says he simply slipped and feels fine, but he takes apixaban and has a small graze on his forehead. What should you do?

answers.text: Do not lift him; keep him still and warm, and call 999, because a knock to the head while on blood-thinning medication can cause dangerous bleeding.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A head injury in someone taking an anticoagulant is an emergency even if they feel well; he must not be moved and needs urgent medical assessment.

answers.text: Help him straight up off the floor, since he says he feels fine and the graze looks small.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. He has hit his head while on a blood thinner; lifting him and assuming he is fine could miss a serious, hidden bleed.

answers.text: Give him a cup of tea and note it in the diary, as there is no need to involve anyone else.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This situation needs a 999 call, not just a diary note; delaying could let a dangerous bleed go untreated.

answers.text: Wait a few hours to see whether he develops a headache before deciding whether to call for help.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Waiting is dangerous with a head injury on anticoagulants; you should call 999 straight away rather than watch and hope.
